idea: Friendly-fraud customer disputes a legitimate large purchase made on a dormant card after Assay's 'innocence' signals (home_region, stable_profile, long_tenure_clean) were explicitly disabled in B29_innocence.md, leaving only R7 able to clear a customer denial.

case.trigger_text: Customer called to dispute an unauthorized online charge of $1,149.99 on a card they state has been kept in a drawer for over a month. Cardholder denies making or authorizing the transaction.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: B29_innocence.md states that home_region, stable_profile, and long_tenure_clean are disabled and only R7 recurring charges can clear a denial. Plus B5_dormant.md gives a 5.65 LR boost for a dormant card waking up. Assay will treat this friendly-fraud buyer's remorse as confirmed fraud and block/report a legitimate customer.

idea: Genuine account takeover where the attacker's final disputed cash-out charge exactly mimics a 30-day monthly recurring subscription ($89.99 on the same home profile) to trick Assay's R7 recurring-charge rule into clearing real fraud, while placing earlier ATO extraction charges outside the 1-hour N7_dispute_episode cap.

case.trigger_text: Customer reported unauthorized activity on their account, specifically disputing the recent $89.99 online transaction and stating their account was compromised over the last day.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: First, the flagged transaction e5 matches e1 from exactly 30 days (720 hours) earlier in amount ($89.99), product, channel, email, device, and region, baiting Assay's R7 recurring-charge rule to clear the denial as legitimate. Second, even if Assay calls it fraud, N7_dispute_episode.md caps dispute episode building to 1 hour around the disputed charge, so e2, e3, and e4 (2 to 18 hours before open) will be excluded and exposure severely undercounted.

idea: Friendly-fraud customer makes a rapid sequence of three small digital micro-purchases followed by a large purchase within 40 minutes on their own card and then disputes the large charge, weaponizing R5 card testing and the 1-hour dispute episode builder against a legitimate customer.

case.trigger_text: Cardholder called to dispute a $689.00 online charge and three preceding small charges from earlier today, claiming they did not authorize any of the transactions.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: The customer bought three in-app currency packs and an expensive item on a new phone and immediately claimed unauthorized use (friendly fraud). Because it matches R5 (3 small online auths within an hour followed by >$100 cleared purchase) and R2 (customer denies), and Assay's innocence signals are disabled, Assay will classify this legitimate customer as high-confidence card_testing fraud and block the card.

idea: Friendly-fraud customer on a shared corporate/family billing arrangement where 4 legitimate cards share the same new desktop device profile and billing region, and one cardholder files a false dispute over $1,000, triggering Assay's B4_cpc / B15_rings detector (under the 15-card cap) to falsely convict and monitor the entire group.

case.trigger_text: Customer on card A disputes $1,280.00 online purchase, stating they never made the booking and do not recognize the charge.

truth.why_it_should_fool_assay: Four family members booked travel together on one desktop computer, and Card A's owner is committing friendly fraud to get their $1,280 back after a change of plans. Because 4 cards (<15 ring cap) share the exact device, email domain, product, and region in a 12-hour window, Assay's ring/CPC/campaign detectors and R2/R6 rules will fire at >0.95 fraud probability, blocking Card A, filing a SAR, and monitoring connected legitimate cards.
